title: Secure Identity & Delegated Access for an AI App (OAuth/OIDC/Okta) and Defend It

teaser.setup: Your AI product authenticates users via an IdP (Okta/Entra) and its agent calls downstream APIs on their behalf. Design the identity architecture and defend the calls under pressure — OIDC, token validation, delegated access, and secrets.
you_will_practice: OIDC login and JWT access-token validation
Where to enforce authorization (data layer, not UI)
Delegated access for agents (on-behalf-of / token exchange)
Secrets, rotation, and least privilege per tool

sample_node.prompt: The agent must call downstream APIs as the user. How do you delegate access safely?
sample_node.model: OAuth2 on-behalf-of / token exchange to mint a scoped, short-lived downstream token — not the agent reusing the user's broad token. Least-privilege scopes per tool, short TTL, and an audit of which identity performed each call. Secrets live in a vault, never in the prompt. Scope-down per hop so a compromised tool can't act broadly.
signals: token exchange / OBO, not broad-token reuse

n1.prompt: Clarify first, then give your one-paragraph identity design for an SPA + API + agent that calls downstream services.
n1.model: Clarify: user population + IdP (Okta/Entra), which downstream APIs, data sensitivity, and session needs. Design: OIDC login with PKCE for the SPA → short-lived access token (JWT) with audience/scope; the API validates signature, exp, aud, iss on every request; identity propagates and authorization is enforced at the data layer; the agent uses OAuth2 token exchange to get scoped downstream tokens; refresh handled server-side; secrets in a vault with rotation. Audit everything.
signals: authz at the data layer + delegated downstream tokens

n2.prompt: Why validate the audience (aud) and issuer (iss) on the token, not just the signature?
n2.model: A valid signature only proves the IdP minted the token — not that it was minted for YOUR service. Without aud/iss checks, a token issued for another service (or a different tenant) could be replayed against yours (a confused-deputy / token-reuse attack). Checking aud ensures the token was meant for this API, and iss ensures it came from the IdP you trust. Also check exp and, where relevant, nonce.
signals: iss pins the trusted IdP; also exp

n3.prompt: Where do you enforce 'this user can only see their own/their tenant's data'? Defend the placement.
n3.model: At the data/retrieval layer, keyed off the verified identity in the token — row-level security or a tenant filter applied before any data is returned. Never rely on the UI or the LLM/agent to filter, and never trust a client-supplied user/tenant id. The token is the source of truth for who the caller is; the data layer is the source of truth for what they may see. Defense in depth: API scope check + data-layer enforcement.
signals: enforce at data layer from the verified token

n4.prompt: The agent must call downstream APIs as the user. How do you delegate access safely?
n4.model: OAuth2 on-behalf-of / token exchange to mint a scoped, short-lived downstream token — not the agent reusing the user's broad token. Least-privilege scopes per tool, short TTL, and an audit of which identity performed each call. Secrets in a vault, never in the prompt. Scope-down per hop so a compromised tool can't act broadly.
signals: token exchange / OBO, not broad-token reuse

n5.prompt: How do you manage the secrets and keys this system depends on?
n5.model: Secrets (client secrets, downstream API keys) live in a managed vault/secret store, injected at runtime — never in code, env files in the repo, or the prompt. Rotate on a schedule and on suspected compromise; prefer short-lived credentials and workload identity over static keys. Validate the IdP's signing keys via JWKS with rotation. Least privilege for the service's own IAM role.
signals: JWKS key rotation; least-privilege service role

n6.prompt: A short-lived access token was leaked in a log. What's the blast radius and what do you do?
n6.model: Blast radius is bounded by the token's short TTL and narrow scope — which is exactly why you issued it that way. Immediate: revoke/rotate the affected credentials and invalidate sessions if needed; scrub logs and fix the log statement that captured it (never log tokens). Investigate via audit for misuse in the window. Prevent: structured logging with redaction, token binding where supported, and alerts on anomalous use. The design (short TTL + least scope) limited the damage.
signals: short TTL + narrow scope bounds the damage

n7.prompt: Where did you assert a choice without the mechanism, the trade-off, or the verification?
checklist: I used OIDC + PKCE + short-lived scoped tokens
I validated signature AND aud/iss/exp, not just signature
I enforced authorization at the data layer from the verified identity
I delegated agent access with scoped token exchange, not broad reuse
I kept secrets in a vault with rotation and redacted logs
